extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in media studies, sociology, and political communication; journalists interested in press effects
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for evaluating newspaper feature treatments, news stories and letters-to-the-editor (illustrated by the Handsworth case), including how images, selection practices and rhetorical styles shape public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing structural causes to surface appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce the definition of the problem from one embracing the hidden mechanisms of housing, poverty and race to one involving simply the surface appearance of dirt and dereliction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: short-circuiting environment/crime relationships by treating litter or derelict houses as signs that 'infect' inhabitants with moral pollution. Instead trace mediations (family, school, job) and structural determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace mediations between environment and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: When linking environment and crime, avoid displacing social ties (family, school, job) into mere pieces; rather examine their functions as structural/cultural institutions mediating effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than inferring direct causation from physical decay to criminality, identify and analyse the intervening social mechanisms that could explain behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causes from effects in feature lists
rubrics_metrics.description: When features list crime, prostitution, poor housing, poverty and inter-racial strife, resist collapsing which are causes and which are effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic requirement: don't allow evocative descriptive lists to stand in for causal explanation; ask 'If the environment determines crime, what determines the environment?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical closure via 'public images'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let a 'public image'—a cluster of impressions and quasi-explanations—replace serious analysis or foreclose further explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'ghetto' or 'new slum' image can condense complex relationships into a graphic but circular definition that halts deeper inquiry; features should avoid using such images as substitutes for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of evocative imagery (e.g., 'ghetto', 'moral decline')
rubrics_metrics.description: Evocative images are powerful rhetorically but often short of serious analysis; they can shift discussion from concrete analysis to generalised analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when imagery is being used to produce rhetorical closure and seek to unpack or contest the analogies and assumptions embedded in the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localise problems only with caution (youth/family redefinitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that redefine environment-based problems as ones of 'youth' or the 'family' may make issues seem amenable to local/pragmatic solutions but risk oversimplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that such redefinitions reposition causes (e.g., from housing/race to lack of recreation or family breakdown) and assess whether this narrows understanding unduly.

rubrics_metrics.name: News defines issues for letters and features (news primacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and features typically 'take off from' the points of newsworthiness first identified in news treatment; news is the primary structure shaping subsequent commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating letters or features, map them back to the news agenda to understand which aspects of the debate are highlighted or constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter columns are editorially selected, not representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of letters is ultimately in the hands of the editor; the column does not provide a representative slice of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat letters-to-the-editor as accurate public-opinion measures; instead evaluate them as curated, rhetorically organised interventions that serve editorial aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match letters to the paper's 'social image' and flavour
rubrics_metrics.description: Different papers' letter pages have distinct 'flavours' and will select letters consistent with the paper's social image and readership (e.g., The Times 'between equals' vs populars addressing 'you').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess letters by whether they fit the paper's assumed conversational universe, class/education assumptions, and intended readership; this shapes both what is printed and who writes in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial 'balance' is an effect, not statistical parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers may print letters on both sides of an issue to achieve a sense of 'balance', but this is an editorial effect rather than a true numerical or representative balance of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a paper's balance, note that selection is strategic (to stimulate debate, show openness) rather than a neutral tally of views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select letters for status of writer and strategic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters will be chosen partly for the status of the writer—'very special people' or grass-roots voices—depending on the paper's orientation and editorial aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of letters by influential figures or identifiable community voices is used to legitimate positions or to demonstrate breadth; evaluate how status is used to shape perceived consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters serve to orchestrate public debate and sustain democratic image
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-to-the-editor help the press organise and orchestrate debate about public questions and sustain the claim that the press is open and acts as a 'fourth estate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat letters as part of a mediated, organised conversation aimed at influencing policy and opinion rather than as spontaneous private communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify rhetorical frame: penological vs wider structural
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters on crime tend to fall into a 'penological' frame (focused on sentencing, deterrence, rehabilitation) or a wider structural/social-frame (linking crime to environment, discrimination, poverty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and evaluate letters by whether they accept the definition of crime and debate control strategies, or whether they broaden the frame to question underlying causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess use of authority and evidence (experts, statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasive letters may quote statistical studies or professional expert experience (prison psychologists, social workers) to support arguments about sentencing and causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the evidential basis of letters: are claims supported by data or professional testimony, and is the evidence used to legitimately extend the debate beyond immediate news points?

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate rhetorical tone and style as ideological signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone and style (plain-speaking, confident common-sense vs longer, argumentative, contextualising prose) often signal traditionalist or liberal positions respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how colloquialism, blunt assertion, or moralizing language function to assert 'everyone knows' truths, versus how more qualified, evidence-based styles argue for less popular conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal experience as persuasive device
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal testimony and appeals to 'ordinary people' or 'personal experience' are frequently employed to undercut abstract reformist arguments or to bolster claims about crime and discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, consider the rhetorical force of lived-experience evidence and whether it is deployed to generalise, contest statistics, or reinforce moral claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of substituting evocative description for causal explanation in features
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that assemble a list of 'pathological symptoms' may be descriptive and evocative but fail to explain causal mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require features to move beyond evocative description (crime, prostitution, poor housing) to specify causal relationships and avoid circular definitions that simply restate the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise ideological functions of imagery and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Images (ghetto, youth, family) perform ideological work by redefining problems in ways that make certain solutions seem natural and foreclose politically sensitive explanations (e.g., structural inequalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically assess which political or ideological positions a given image naturalises and what lines of political inquiry or policy are thereby closed off.
